design_detail: Short narrative review in the Resident Short Reviews series of Archives of Pathology & Laboratory Medicine (4 pages, 27 references) by a pathology resident and a senior pathologist at Houston Methodist Hospital, describing vasculitis attributed to levamisole in people who use levamisole-adulterated cocaine: clinical, histological and laboratory features, differential diagnosis, and treatment. Five illustrations (one clinical photograph, four skin-biopsy micrographs) without a stated source patient, and one summary table. No search strategy, selection criteria or appraisal.
can_establish: How pathologists described the skin and laboratory picture of vasculitis attributed to levamisole in cocaine as of 2014 (retiform purpura; microvascular fibrin thrombi with or without leukocytoclastic vasculitis; neutropenia; ANCA and other autoantibodies) and which differential diagnoses they consider.
cannot_establish: How often this vasculitis occurs among people who use cocaine, whether its incidence is rising (no data are given), that levamisole rather than cocaine itself is the cause in a given patient (the review says testing for levamisole is unnecessary for diagnosis), or how well any treatment works.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). Cited evidence: case reports and small series (refs 5–12, 16–18, 26, 27), a CDC report and toxicology studies on prevalence (refs 3, 13–15), and references on pathogenesis and ANCA testing (refs 19–25).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No search or selection criteria stated.
sample.selection_effects: Author-selected literature, mostly case reports, which favour dramatic and well-documented cases. The source of the five illustrations (which patient, whether levamisole was tested) is not stated (p. 1059).

exposure.measurement: As summarized: cocaine use by history or by urine immunoassay for benzoylecgonine, confirmed by GC-MS or LC-MS/MS; levamisole detected by mass spectrometry in some reports (refs 11, 12, 13), but the review states that testing for levamisole is not required for diagnosis (p. 1060).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not reported. The review states that about 70% of cocaine in the US contains levamisole (refs 3, 13, 14; p. 1058).

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable (review). Tests described: skin-biopsy histology; blood counts (leukopenia below 4000/µL, neutropenia below 1500/µL, agranulocytosis below 500/µL); erythrocyte sedimentation rate; coagulation studies; ANCA by indirect immunofluorescence on ethanol-fixed neutrophils, confirmed by proteinase-3 and myeloperoxidase immunoassays; antinuclear antibody; lupus anticoagulant; toxicology (p. 1060).
outcomes.operationalization: No case definition; the entity is described by retiform purpura, the histology, the laboratory findings and a history of cocaine use (Table, p. 1061).

analysis.effect_sizes: None computed. Second-hand figures: male-to-female ratio 1:3 and mean age at presentation 44 years (ref. 12, p. 1058); about 70% of US cocaine contains levamisole (p. 1058); levamisole half-life 5.6 hours (ref. 26, p. 1060).

interpretation_gap.results_show: A clinicopathological description, drawn from case reports and small series, of a retiform purpuric rash with microvascular thrombi and/or leukocytoclastic vasculitis, neutropenia and autoantibodies in people who use cocaine, which in nearly all reported cases resolved once cocaine use stopped.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract cites a "rising incidence" (p. 1058) and the Conclusion an "increasing incidence" (p. 1061) of the entity; no incidence or trend data are given, only the statement that detection of levamisole in cocaine has increased (p. 1058). The Introduction says that finding levamisole by urine toxicology and mass spectrometry in patients with suspected vasculitis confirmed it as the cause (p. 1058); but if about 70% of cocaine contains levamisole (the review's own figure, p. 1058), most patients who use cocaine will test positive whatever caused their rash, so detection shows exposure, not cause. The review's diagnostic advice not to test for levamisole because it is so common (p. 1060) means cases are attributed to levamisole by assumption. The treatment advice (stop cocaine; it may be prudent to avoid corticosteroids because of neutropenia and wound infection) is the authors' opinion for hospital care, resting on case reports (p. 1060).

timeline.event: Levamisole-induced vasculitis described in a patient treated for rheumatoid arthritis (Macfarlane & Bacon, ref. 2, as cited p. 1058)
CDC report of agranulocytosis associated with cocaine use in four states, March 2008 to November 2009 (ref. 3)
Walsh et al. (ref. 11): retiform purpura in people using cocaine, with evidence the authors took to incriminate levamisole
Narrative review of agranulocytosis and other consequences of levamisole-contaminated cocaine

replication.where_it_stands: A teaching summary for pathologists. The histological description is consistent across the cited cases; the attribution to levamisole, and any statement about frequency or trend, are not quantified in it. Claims should cite primary case series with testing data.

funding.declared_conflicts: The authors state that they have no relevant financial interest in the products or companies described in the article (p. 1058).
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Pathology and Genomic Medicine, Houston Methodist Hospital, and Weill Cornell Medical College (p. 1058); a resident-authored short review. None of the cited studies is by the authors.

what_would_settle_it: A case–control study of people who use cocaine with and without retiform purpura or neutropenia, with levamisole and cocaine measured in both groups and standard histological and laboratory definitions; for treatment, a comparative study of corticosteroids versus none in confirmed cases.

domains.note: Case reports are summarized without appraisal, and detection of levamisole in case series is described as confirming the cause.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: None of the cited studies is by the authors.
Pathogenesis is labelled uncertain and the corticosteroid advice is framed as prudence, but a rising incidence and a confirmed cause are stated as facts.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on cause and frequency (cocaine itself as an alternative cause, and the absence of incidence data, are under-represented)
domains.note: Differential diagnoses of other vasculitides are covered well, but whether cocaine itself contributes, and how rare the condition is among people exposed, are not discussed.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to narrative reviews (METHODS §5.3); the editors' checklist gives high concern overall because there is no systematic search and no appraisal of the case literature. As a description of histological and laboratory features for pathologists the review is clear and properly sourced. Claims may cite it for the clinical, histological and laboratory picture and the differential diagnosis; not for frequency, trend, causation, or treatment effects.

key_findings.finding: Clinical picture: a tender, purpuric rash in a retiform or stellate pattern, with or without central necrosis, on the extremities, trunk, nasal tip, digits, cheeks or ears; bullae are not uncommon and skin sloughing allows bacterial superinfection; ear and digit lesions have been reported to self-amputate.
Demography cited: predilection for women (male-to-female ratio 1:3) and mean age at presentation 44 years, both cited to one paper (ref. 12) whose title describes a single patient.
key_findings.note: The number of cases behind the ratio and the mean age is not given.

key_findings.finding: Laboratory findings: leukopenia (<4000/µL), neutropenia (<1500/µL) including agranulocytosis (<500/µL), raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate, normal coagulation, and autoantibodies including p- and c-ANCA, antinuclear antibody and lupus anticoagulant.

Histology: leukocytoclastic vasculitis of small vessels and multiple fibrin thrombi in small vessels of the superficial and deep dermis, classically both but often only one; microvascular fibrin thrombi are the most consistent feature, and some authors consider the combination relatively specific; epidermal changes depend on the biopsy site.
key_findings.locator: Pathologic Features, 1st paragraph (begins p. 1058, continues on p. 1059); Figures 2–5 (p. 1059)

key_findings.finding: Bone marrow in patients with agranulocytosis: myeloid hypoplasia, mild megakaryocyte hyperplasia and increased marrow plasma cells, with circulating plasmacytoid lymphocytes.
Pathogenesis is uncertain; an immune complex–mediated process is favoured on skin immunofluorescence, and for agranulocytosis a hapten mechanism has been suggested.

ANCA specificity: antibodies against human neutrophil elastase are cited as strongly associated with cocaine-induced lesions and as possibly helping to distinguish levamisole-induced vasculitis from other ANCA-associated vasculitides.
key_findings.note: Per its title, the cited study (ref. 25, 2004) concerns cocaine-induced midline destructive lesions, not levamisole vasculitis.

key_findings.finding: Testing: levamisole half-life 5.6 hours; detectable by GC-MS but described as not necessary for diagnosis; cocaine use is screened by urine immunoassay for benzoylecgonine and confirmed by GC-MS or LC-MS/MS; levamisole testing is described as not required because levamisole is so prevalent in cocaine.

Differential diagnosis: ANCA-associated vasculitides (granulomatosis with polyangiitis, microscopic polyangiitis, Churg-Strauss syndrome), septic vasculitis, disseminated intravascular coagulation, cryoglobulinaemia, warfarin-induced skin necrosis and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia; histological overlap makes clinical correlation essential.

Treatment and prognosis: the ideal treatment is undetermined; nearly all cases resolve once cocaine use stops; corticosteroids have not been shown to help and the authors suggest it may be prudent to avoid them because of neutropenia and wound infection; plasmapheresis appears only in case reports; some patients needed debridement, skin grafting or amputation.

Context stated: about 70% of US cocaine contains levamisole; levamisole has been detected in cocaine since 2003, with detection increasing; medical use has ended (the review says the FDA banned it in 2000), so current cases are attributed exclusively to adulterated cocaine.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that the FDA banned levamisole in the US in 2000 (p. 1058) is cited to refs 3 and 4, and ref. 4 is a 1999 paper that cannot document a 2000 ban; another review read in this round (Buchanan & Lavonas; card sc_buchanan_2012) says instead that levamisole remained FDA-approved as adjuvant colon-cancer treatment but was no longer marketed for human use in the US.
reporting_issues.consequence: The regulatory history should come from a primary regulatory source, not from either review.

reporting_issues.issue: The sex ratio (1:3) and mean age (44 years) are cited to a single paper whose title describes one patient (ref. 12).
reporting_issues.consequence: The figures cannot be traced to a number of cases; do not cite them from this review.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and Conclusion describe a rising or increasing incidence (pp. 1058, 1061) without incidence or trend data; the only trend stated concerns detection of levamisole in cocaine (p. 1058).
reporting_issues.consequence: Not citable as evidence of a rising incidence.

reporting_issues.issue: The source of the clinical photograph and the four micrographs (which patient, consent, whether levamisole was detected) is not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: The images illustrate typical features but cannot be taken as confirmed cases.

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record), Archives of Pathology & Laboratory Medicine 139(8), pp. 1058–1061 (all pages read on 150-dpi renderings, p. 1059 also at 300 dpi; Figures 1–5 are images, described from their legends; the summary table checked on the rendered page; no supplement).
